title: A merge into main is a release, and it names its bump
description:
Day-to-day work lands on the configured target branch. Reaching `main` is a separate act the user asks for, and it is a release: it must name patch, minor or major.

What is already here: .changeset/config.json pins `baseBranch: "main"` and `commit: false`; releases run through a version-packages pull request (see `chore: version packages (#6)`) and a staged npm publish (docs/adr/0053). Nothing today connects a SOBER node, or a merge, to a bump — a release can ship with no changeset and no version move, silently.

Close that: make the bump an explicit step on the way to `main`, wire it into the changeset the release pull request consumes, and write the ADR that says a merge into `main` is a release. CLAUDE.md already states the rule for agents; the ADR is the record behind it.

Acceptance: a merge into `main` cannot happen without a named bump, and the resulting version move matches the bump that was named. Tests land with the code.

brief.approach:
Score 5: mostly a CI gate and an ADR, but it is the release path, so getting the gate's condition wrong either blocks every pull request or protects nothing.

**Read what is already here before writing anything.** `.changeset/config.json` pins `baseBranch: "main"` and `commit: false`. `.github/workflows/ci.yml:44-50` already has the step — `a changeset, or nothing to release` — conditioned on `github.base_ref == 'main'`, skipping Renovate and `changeset-release/*` branches, running `changeset status --since=origin/main`. `scripts/release.mjs` stages the npm publish and tags (ADR 0053). So the wiring from changeset to published version exists and is not this node's to rebuild.

**The one real gap.** `changeset status --since` succeeds when a changeset file exists, whatever bump it names — and it also succeeds when nothing in the range is a publishable change. What it cannot say is that the bump was *chosen by the person releasing* rather than left over from some branch. Close it at the narrowest point rather than building a release command:

1. **Make the step's failure say what to do.** `changeset status` failing today prints changesets' own message. Add a `continue-on-error`-free step wrapper (or an `if: failure()` step immediately after) that prints, in the repository's own voice: this pull request targets `main`, which is a release; name the bump with `pnpm exec changeset`, choosing patch, minor or major, and commit the file it writes. A gate a person cannot act on is a gate they route around.
2. **Assert the bump is real, not empty.** After `changeset status`, add a step on the same condition that reads the changeset files added in this range (`git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD -- .changeset/*.md`) and fails when none was added — `changeset status` passes on a changeset that was already on `main`, which is exactly the silent release the node describes. Keep it to `@besober/cli`: ADR 0007 makes it the only published package, so a changeset naming anything else is not a release and should say so.

**Do not build a `sober release` command.** The board's rule (CLAUDE.md) is that a merge into `main` happens only when the user asks for one, and the bump is their call at that moment. A command that performs it invites a session to run it. The gate belongs in CI, where a human pressing merge is already the trigger.

**The ADR.** `docs/adr/0059-a-merge-into-main-is-a-release.md` — 0058 is the highest today, so 0059 is free; check `ls docs/adr` before writing, since another node may take it first. Follow the shape of the ADRs beside it (context, decision, consequences, and the alternatives that were rejected and why). It records what CLAUDE.md already tells agents: work lands on `dispatch.base`; reaching `main` is a separate act the user asks for; that merge is a release and names patch, minor or major; a node never writes a changeset, because a node publishes nothing. Cite the second decision bound to this node for the reasoning, including its cost — the bump is chosen far from the change, so a breaking change buried among twenty nodes is easy to bill as a patch — and say what the CI gate does and does not catch. Reference ADR 0053 for what happens after the version moves, and ADR 0007 for why one package.

**Tests.** CI steps are not unit-testable here, so prove the condition rather than the runner: add to `test/integration/ratchets.test.ts` (which already asserts facts about repository configuration) two cases — `.github/workflows/ci.yml` contains a step gated on `base_ref == 'main'` that requires a changeset, and `.changeset/config.json` still pins `baseBranch: "main"` so the `--since` range means what the step assumes. Assert the ADR file exists and names the three bump words, the way the repository already pins prose facts in `test/integration/docs.test.ts` (landed in `d08ef429`) — read that file first and match its register.

Nothing in `packages/` changes: no core, no schema, no CLI, no MCP tool, no dashboard. This node is CI, one ADR, and the two assertions that keep both honest.

acceptance.proves: the changeset gate is still conditioned on a pull request into main and `.changeset/config.json` still pins baseBranch to main — the two facts the gate's `--since` range depends on
the ADR exists and names all three bumps — the record behind the rule CLAUDE.md already states for agents
the gate fires only on the merge that actually releases, so a pull request into development is not asked for a bump it has no business naming

acceptance.run: ! git grep -qi "'release'" -- packages/cli/src/index.ts || git grep -q "release <node" -- packages/cli/src/index.ts
acceptance.proves: no `sober release` command was added — the existing `release <node>` is giving a claim back, and performing a release stays something only a human does by merging
nothing in packages/ or apps/ changed: this node is CI, one ADR and its assertions, and it publishes nothing and moves no version
